- For **acute traumatic SCI**, the 2024 guideline weakly suggests augmenting MAP to **at least 75–80 mmHg**, but **not actively beyond 90–95 mmHg**.
- Suggested duration is **3–7 days**, chosen according to physiology and risk; evidence is very low certainty.
- Avoid hypoxaemia and sustained hypotension; do not assume these targets apply to every neurogenic shock patient.
- Choice of vasopressor is individualised; no proven single best agent.
> **Closing point:** Maintain cord perfusion.

items.title: What is the MAP target in acute spinal cord injury?
items.q: What is the MAP target in acute spinal cord injury?
items.a:
- The 2024 traumatic-SCI guideline suggests a lower augmented MAP limit 75–80 mmHg and no active augmentation above 90–95.
- Suggested duration is 3–7 days, individualised; both recommendations are weak with very low certainty.
- Exclude bleeding and maintain appropriate volume, oxygenation and cord perfusion.
- Choose pressor by physiology and adverse effects; no agent has proven universal superiority.
> **Closing point:** This updates the older fixed 85–90 for seven days rule.

items.title: What are the effects of adrenaline at different doses?
items.q: What are the effects of adrenaline at different doses?
items.a:
- Low dose: beta-1 and beta-2 effects.
- High dose: alpha-1 vasoconstriction.
- Raises lactate.
- Used in anaphylaxis and arrest.
> **Closing point:** Dose-dependent receptor profile.

items.title: When do you use dobutamine?
items.q: When do you use dobutamine?
items.a:
- Low cardiac output with adequate MAP.
- Septic cardiomyopathy.
- Beta-1 inotropy.
- Can cause hypotension and arrhythmia.
> **Closing point:** Inotrope, not vasopressor.

items.title: What are the effects of milrinone?
items.q: What are the effects of milrinone?
items.a:
- PDE-III inhibitor.
- Inotropy, lusitropy and vasodilatation.
- Reduces pulmonary vascular resistance.
- Renally cleared and may cause hypotension.
> **Closing point:** Inodilator that works despite beta-blockade.

items.title: How does levosimendan work?
items.q: How does levosimendan work?
items.a:
- Calcium sensitiser.
- K-ATP channel opening.
- Effects last up to a week.
- Evidence is mixed.
> **Closing point:** Calcium sensitiser with long action.

items.title: What is methylene blue used for?
items.q: What is methylene blue used for?
items.a:
- Vasoplegia after bypass.
- Inhibits nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase.
- A specialist vasoplegia regimen may use **1–2 mg/kg over 15–30 min**, with monitoring; not a rapid unqualified push.
- Avoid with serotonergic drugs and G6PD deficiency.
> **Closing point:** Rescue for vasoplegia.

items.title: Which vasopressors do you use for hypotension after induction?
items.q: Which vasopressors do you use for hypotension after induction?
items.a:
- Phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms.
- Small IV ephedrine boluses can suit transient vasodilatation with modest bradycardia. Severe bradycardia or instability needs immediate resuscitation and cause-specific treatment.
- Noradrenaline infusion.
- Choose by heart rate and cardiac output.
> **Closing point:** Match the drug to the haemodynamic problem.

items.title: What are the receptor effects of noradrenaline?
items.q: What are the receptor effects of noradrenaline?
items.a:
- Strong alpha-1 vasoconstriction.
- Moderate beta-1 effect.
- Raises MAP and SVR.
- First-line vasopressor.
> **Closing point:** The standard vasopressor.

items.title: When do you use vasopressin?
items.q: When do you use vasopressin?
items.a:
- Add-on in septic shock and vasoplegia.
- Acts on V1 receptors.
- Often used at ~0.03 units/min as an adjunct, according to local protocol; it is **not** an unconditional fixed dose for every indication.
- Reduces catecholamine need.
> **Closing point:** Catecholamine-sparing.

items.title: What are the risks of dopamine?
items.q: What are the risks of dopamine?
items.a:
- More arrhythmias than noradrenaline.
- SOAP II showed more arrhythmias with dopamine, with a concerning cardiogenic-shock subgroup mortality signal; there was not a significant overall mortality difference.
- Variable receptor effects.
- Rarely first choice.
> **Closing point:** SOAP II changed practice.

items.title: What are the dangers of extravasation of vasopressors?
items.q: What are the dangers of extravasation of vasopressors?
items.a:
- Tissue necrosis.
- Central access is preferred for prolonged/high-dose treatment, but **appropriately diluted peripheral noradrenaline is acceptable for urgent short-term use with vigilant site monitoring**; do not delay shock treatment while obtaining a central line.
- Use a reliable proximal peripheral line, infusion pump, appropriate concentration and frequent inspection per local policy.
- If extravasation is suspected: **stop the infusion, leave the cannula initially to aspirate (do not flush)**, restart via safe access, elevate/assess the limb and urgently follow the local extravasation pathway, including phentolamine where available.
> **Closing point:** Check the cannula.

items.title: Which vasopressor suits vasodilatation with bradycardia?
items.q: Which vasopressor suits vasodilatation with bradycardia?
items.a:
- Ephedrine may suit transient vasodilatation with a low heart rate.
- Severe symptomatic bradycardia also needs chronotropic treatment (ANZCOR atropine 500–600 micrograms IV, then escalation as indicated).
- Noradrenaline can support vascular tone but does not reliably correct profound bradycardia; adrenaline/pacing may be required.
- Avoid relying on a pure alpha agonist alone when bradycardia is limiting output, and treat bleeding/high block or other triggers.
> **Closing point:** Support both rate and perfusion by the actual mechanism.

items.title: Can vasopressors be given peripherally?
items.q: Can vasopressors be given peripherally?
items.a:
- Yes: start urgently needed noradrenaline through a suitable monitored peripheral line rather than waiting for central access.
- Use the standard local concentration, a patent visible appropriate cannula, pump, backup route and frequent site checks.
- Central access depends on reliability, dose, duration and monitoring; there is no universal 24-hour rule.
- For extravasation stop that route, do not flush, aspirate initially with the cannula retained, secure alternative support and follow the pharmacy antidote/escalation protocol.
> **Closing point:** Early perfusion support requires a reliable surveillance system.

items.title: What is lusitropy and why is it distinct from inotropy?
items.q: What is lusitropy and why is it distinct from inotropy?
items.a:
- **Inotropy** increases the force of contraction; **lusitropy** increases the rate/quality of myocardial relaxation in diastole by improving calcium handling.
- Beta-agonists and PDE3 inhibition can provide positive lusitropy; milrinone combines inotropy/lusitropy with systemic and pulmonary vasodilation.
- In a stiff LV/HFpEF, faster HR, lower SVR or ischaemia may worsen filling despite improved cellular relaxation.
- Preserve sinus rhythm and appropriate diastolic filling time; select medication to correct the actual defect rather than assuming “lusitrope = HFpEF treatment”.
> **Closing point:** Good relaxation is not equivalent to a faster heart.

items.title: Why might noradrenaline increase MAP but reduce cardiac output?
items.q: Why might noradrenaline increase MAP but reduce cardiac output?
items.a: - Venoconstriction can recruit venous blood and improve preload, while arterial constriction supports pressure. But increased LV afterload, RV dysfunction or excessive vasoconstriction can reduce forward flow. Check SV/CO and perfusion, not just MAP; a drug response depends on the starting physiology.

items.title: How do you safely convert vasopressin infusion units?
items.q: How do you safely convert vasopressin infusion units?
items.a:
- 0.01–0.04 units/min equals 0.6–2.4 units/hour.
- Do not confuse units/min with units/hour or micrograms/kg/min; check prescription, pump and local preparation.
- Use a protocol-specific titration plan with surveillance for digital, mesenteric and other ischaemic effects.
- An improved MAP does not prove better flow, and relative pulmonary sparing is dose-dependent.
> **Closing point:** Check the time unit before checking the pump rate.

items.title: What is pulsus paradoxus?
items.q: What is pulsus paradoxus?
items.a:
- An inspiratory decrease in systolic BP >10 mmHg during spontaneous breathing.
- It reflects exaggerated respiratory ventricular interaction/filling changes and can occur in tamponade or severe obstructive lung disease.
- Its absence does not exclude loculated postoperative tamponade, and positive-pressure ventilation changes the pattern.
- Interpret the arterial waveform and respiration together with the whole clinical and echo assessment.
> **Closing point:** A useful physiological sign with context-dependent limitations.

items.title: What is the technique for ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis?
items.q: What is the technique for ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis?
items.a:
- Use ultrasound to select the **shortest safe accessible pericardial fluid pocket** (apical, parasternal or subxiphoid)—not a mandatory subxiphoid track.
- Under asepsis, local anaesthesia and appropriate monitoring, track the needle tip under real-time ultrasound where feasible and aspirate carefully.
- Confirm intrapericardial position by imaging; agitated saline contrast may help if uncertain (blood aspiration alone is insufficient).
- Place a pigtail drain using a safe guidewire technique, relieve haemodynamic obstruction, then monitor for recurrence or decompression syndrome in chronic large effusions.
> **Closing point:** Choose the image-defined safe route; surgery for clotted traumatic/postsurgical blood.

items.title: What are the signs of cardiac tamponade?
items.q: What are the signs of cardiac tamponade?
items.a:
- Beck triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds.
- Pulsus paradoxus.
- Falling drain output after cardiac surgery.
- Echo may show chamber collapse, but high right-sided pressure, ventilation or loculated postoperative clot can mask it; absence does not exclude tamponade.
> **Closing point:** Rate of accumulation matters.

items.title: What are the haemodynamic goals in tamponade?
items.q: What are the haemodynamic goals in tamponade?
items.a:
- Preserve venous return and avoid unnecessary vasodilation; a **small cautious fluid challenge** may be a bridge if underfilled but repeated fluid is not definitive treatment.
- Maintain compensatory HR/contractility and systemic pressure while arranging **urgent drainage**.
- Avoid vasodilators and positive pressure.
- Drain urgently.
> **Closing point:** Fast, full and tight.

items.title: How should anaesthesia be induced in tamponade?
items.q: How should anaesthesia be induced in tamponade?
items.a:
- Preserve spontaneous ventilation if possible.
- Ketamine with vasopressor ready.
- Surgeon scrubbed and ready.
- Avoid high PEEP.
> **Closing point:** Positive pressure reduces filling.

items.title: What are the complications of pericardiocentesis?
items.q: What are the complications of pericardiocentesis?
items.a:
- Coronary or myocardial laceration.
- Arrhythmia and pneumothorax.
- Liver injury.
- Fails in clotted blood.
> **Closing point:** Surgery for clots.

items.title: How does traumatic tamponade differ from medical or postoperative tamponade?
items.q: How does traumatic tamponade differ from medical or postoperative tamponade?
items.a:
- **Medical effusion:** image-guided catheter drainage may be definitive; in a large chronic effusion avoid unnecessary rapid complete emptying because of decompression syndrome.
- **Post-cardiac surgery:** loculated clot may compress a chamber with little free fluid; prompt TOE and **surgical re-exploration** are usually preferable when unstable.
- **Penetrating trauma:** presume an active bleeding cardiac injury and arrange **urgent surgical pericardial opening/repair** with haemostatic resuscitation; a needle may not drain clot or stop bleeding.
- Support pressure/oxygenation while definitive decompression is arranged; avoid delaying surgery with serial fluid boluses.
> **Closing point:** Identify the cause of the effusion, not just the presence of fluid.

items.title: What is your first response to a sudden drop in blood pressure under anaesthesia?
items.q: What is your first response to a sudden drop in blood pressure under anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Confirm the arterial/cuff reading and check for an actual pulse; call for help if severe.
- Give 100% oxygen, assess ventilation and reduce excessive anaesthetic depth **without permitting awareness**.
- Check HR/rhythm, ETCO₂, airway pressure, bleeding and recent drugs; perform focused echo if unexplained.
- Give a **cause-appropriate vasopressor as a bridge**; only give fluid when a deficit is likely and tolerated, and replace blood for haemorrhage. Reassess perfusion and stroke volume.
> **Closing point:** Treat and think at the same time.

items.title: What is the Bezold–Jarisch reflex?
items.q: What is the Bezold–Jarisch reflex?
items.a:
- Underfilled ventricle contracts vigorously.
- Mechanoreceptors trigger vagal response.
- Bradycardia, vasodilatation and hypotension.
- Restore venous return, reduce the provoking stimulus and use atropine/appropriate vasopressor; severe bradycardic shock may need early adrenaline. Give fluid only when indicated and tolerated.
> **Closing point:** A paradoxical vagal reflex.

items.title: What did Walsh and colleagues find about intraoperative MAP?
items.q: What did Walsh and colleagues find about intraoperative MAP?
items.a:
- Walsh studied about 33,000 noncardiac-surgery patients.
- MAP <55 mmHg was associated with myocardial injury and AKI, with risk increasing by duration.
- Observational design and residual confounding limit causal inference; it does not prove a universal safe floor or treatment regimen.
- Use it with current guidance and randomised target trials.
> **Closing point:** Association informs vigilance, not a single universal prescription.

items.title: Why should you not start a beta-blocker on the morning of surgery?
items.q: Why should you not start a beta-blocker on the morning of surgery?
items.a:
- POISE tested initiation of a relatively high-dose extended-release metoprolol regimen shortly before surgery.
- It reduced MI but increased clinically important hypotension, stroke and death.
- Continue established beta-blockade when appropriate; avoid withdrawal.
- If a new indication exists, assess and start sufficiently early for titration rather than on the morning of surgery.
> **Closing point:** Continue appropriately; new initiation needs time and assessment.

items.title: What blood pressure target do you aim for during anaesthesia?
items.q: What blood pressure target do you aim for during anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Avoid sustained severe hypotension. **ACC/AHA 2024:** MAP ≥60–65/SBP ≥90 minimum; **AoA/BIHS 2026:** commonly used higher-risk targets MAP >70 and/or SBP >100. Individualise; do not transfer elective guidance uncritically to emergency shock.
- **“Within 20% of baseline” is not a validated universal requirement.** Consider chronic hypertension and the patient’s autoregulation.
- Higher perfusion pressure may be needed with raised venous, intracranial or compartment pressure, cerebral vascular disease or ongoing ischaemia.
- Assess CO, CRT, lactate trend and organ function, not MAP alone.
> **Closing point:** Avoid severe/prolonged hypotension and individualise to actual perfusion.

items.title: What did IMPROVE-multi add to perioperative BP-target evidence?
items.q: What did IMPROVE-multi add to perioperative BP-target evidence?
items.a:
- A 2025 multicentre trial compared preoperative nighttime-MAP-based individualised targets with routine MAP ≥65 in high-risk major abdominal surgery.
- The early AKI/myocardial-injury/nonfatal-arrest/death composite was not significantly improved.
- It tested one strategy, so it does not prove hypotension is harmless or abolish disease-specific individualisation.
- Assess a defensible pressure floor and actual perfusion rather than applying a universal percentage-of-baseline rule.
> **Closing point:** Distinguish the tested strategy from the general aim of avoiding harmful hypotension.

items.title: What are the common causes of intraoperative hypotension?
items.q: What are the common causes of intraoperative hypotension?
items.a:
- Anaesthetic vasodilatation and myocardial depression.
- Hypovolaemia and bleeding.
- Cardiac: arrhythmia, ischaemia, valve disease.
- Anaphylaxis, embolism, pneumothorax and sepsis.
> **Closing point:** Work through by mechanism.

items.title: What are the harms of intraoperative hypotension?
items.q: What are the harms of intraoperative hypotension?
items.a:
- Myocardial injury.
- Acute kidney injury.
- Stroke and delirium.
- Deeper/longer episodes are **associated** with greater morbidity and mortality; observational associations do not establish causality for every outcome.
> **Closing point:** Duration and depth both matter.

items.title: How do you assess a patient with severe preoperative hypertension?
items.q: How do you assess a patient with severe preoperative hypertension?
items.a:
- Look for end-organ damage.
- Repeat measurement; check medications.
- Exclude secondary causes.
- Name the guideline: **2026 AoA/BIHS uses clinic <180/120** (home <175/115) to permit planned surgery without documented primary-care normotension; other guidance uses 180/110. Persistent 210/120 before elective surgery warrants deferral/optimisation, and acute organ injury requires emergency treatment.
> **Closing point:** Acute end-organ injury changes urgency; a number alone does not define emergency.

items.title: Which antihypertensives do you continue on the day of surgery?
items.q: Which antihypertensives do you continue on the day of surgery?
items.a:
- Continue beta-blockers.
- Continue calcium-channel blockers.
- **AoA/BIHS 2026 normally continues ACEI/ARB. ACC/AHA 2024 permits omission for 24 h in selected elevated-risk noncardiac surgery for controlled hypertension; continuation is reasonable in HFrEF.** Follow the applicable protocol and document the reason.
- Continue clonidine.
> **Closing point:** Avoid withdrawal rebound.

items.title: How do you blunt the hypertensive response to laryngoscopy?
items.q: How do you blunt the hypertensive response to laryngoscopy?
items.a:
- Opioid such as fentanyl or remifentanil.
- Esmolol or lignocaine.
- Adequate depth of anaesthesia.
- Consider a supraglottic device only when appropriate to the surgery, airway and aspiration risk; it is not a substitute for necessary tracheal intubation.
> **Closing point:** Deepen and block.

items.title: What are the secondary causes of hypertension relevant to anaesthesia?
items.q: What are the secondary causes of hypertension relevant to anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Phaeochromocytoma.
- Renal artery stenosis and renal disease.
- Conn syndrome and Cushing syndrome.
- Drugs and pre-eclampsia.
> **Closing point:** Look when it is severe or young.

items.title: How do you treat a hypertensive emergency?
items.q: How do you treat a hypertensive emergency?
items.a:
- Confirm end-organ damage.
- Titratable IV agent: labetalol, GTN or nicardipine.
- In many hypertensive emergencies avoid an abrupt fall (often no more than ~25% MAP initially), **but targets and pace differ in aortic dissection, pregnancy and specific neurological emergencies**.
- Monitor closely with appropriate invasive pressure/critical-care support and treat the organ-specific cause.
> **Closing point:** Slow, controlled reduction.

items.title: Why does hypotension occur after spinal anaesthesia?
items.q: Why does hypotension occur after spinal anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Sympathetic block causes vasodilatation.
- Reduced preload and cardiac accelerator block.
- Bezold–Jarisch reflex.
- Worse in the elderly and hypovolaemic.
> **Closing point:** Vasodilatation plus bradycardia.

items.title: How do you manage hypotension in a patient on ACE inhibitors?
items.q: How do you manage hypotension in a patient on ACE inhibitors?
items.a:
- Vasopressin or noradrenaline for refractory vasoplegia.
- Fluid and phenylephrine.
- Review hypotension and reason for ACEI/ARB, rather than making withholding universal; support preload only if appropriate.
- Methylene blue is a specialist rescue agent for selected severe vasoplegia, not routine first-line induction treatment.
> **Closing point:** Renin–angiotensin blockade blunts the response.

items.title: What does the Blue Book argue about routine vasoconstrictor use for intraoperative hypotension?
items.q: What does the Blue Book argue about routine vasoconstrictor use for intraoperative hypotension?
items.a:
- The 2023 authored perspective cautions that pressure is not flow and questions reflex vasoconstrictor use.
- Treat its physiological arguments critically: dynamic LVOTO may benefit from increased SVR, and pressors have clear cause-specific indications.
- Observational hypotension associations do not prove a particular treatment benefit; randomised target trials also exist.
- Use the chapter alongside contemporary guidelines, physiology and flow/perfusion reassessment.
> **Closing point:** Restore an appropriate pressure and check that perfusion improves.

items.title: What is the safe threshold for proceeding with elective surgery in hypertension?
items.q: What is the safe threshold for proceeding with elective surgery in hypertension?
items.a:
- There is no pressure that alone guarantees safety: repeat accurately and assess acute organ injury, urgency and overall risk.
- AoA/BIHS 2026 permits elective surgery without documented primary-care normotension if clinic BP <180/120 or home/ambulatory BP <175/115.
- ACC/AHA 2024 uses a different ≥180/110 framework for selected elevated-risk surgery; name the guideline and follow local policy.
- Avoid rapid preoperative lowering of chronic asymptomatic hypertension simply to cross a threshold.
> **Closing point:** Apply a named pathway, not a universal “safe BP”.

items.title: How should you approach hypotension and hypertension in PACU?
items.q: How should you approach hypotension and hypertension in PACU?
items.a:
- **Hypotension:** check actual BP/pulse, ABC, depth of sedation, bleeding/drains, vasodilation/neuraxial effects, sepsis, MI/arrhythmia, anaphylaxis, PE and volume loss; use Hb/gas/ECG/echo as appropriate. Treat cause, not just the cuff.
- **Hypertension:** first look for pain, hypoxia, hypercapnia, agitation, urinary retention, shivering, nausea and missed chronic drugs; correct triggers before escalating IV antihypertensives.
- Search for **acute target-organ injury** (myocardial ischaemia, pulmonary oedema, neurological signs or aortic emergency), and adapt BP targets to recent neurovascular/cardiac surgery.
- Reassess ventilation, perfusion and recovery destination after treatment.
> **Closing point:** A hypertensive emergency requires organ injury, not just a very high number.

items.title: 1. Explain stressed venous volume and mean systemic filling pressure. How can…
items.q: Explain stressed venous volume and mean systemic filling pressure. How can noradrenaline improve venous return without giving more fluid, and why might cardiac output nevertheless fall?
items.a:
### The venous reservoir and return gradient

- Unstressed volume fills the vascular space without generating appreciable recoil pressure; stressed volume stretches vessels and generates pressure.
- These are functional concepts that change with venous tone, not two anatomically separate tanks.
- **Mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsf)** describes the equilibrium pressure in the systemic circulation at zero flow.
- In a simplified model, **venous return = (Pmsf − right atrial pressure)/resistance to venous return**.
- At steady state venous return equals CO.

### Vasodilation and hypovolaemia

Venodilation increases capacitance and shifts volume towards the unstressed compartment, potentially lowering Pmsf/venous return without a fall in total blood volume. Actual haemorrhage reduces available volume. These can coexist. Raising CVP alone does not establish improved filling or flow; it can indicate failing RV ejection or increased intrathoracic pressure.

### Effects of noradrenaline

Venoconstriction, especially of capacitance beds, can recruit unstressed volume and increase Pmsf/preload. Arterial vasoconstriction restores perfusion pressure, while modest beta-1 effects and improved coronary pressure may support contraction. If the ventricle is preload responsive and able to eject, CO may increase without an additional fluid bolus.

The response is not guaranteed. Increased LV afterload may reduce SV in a poorly contracting heart; increased resistance to venous return, RV dysfunction, excessive vasoconstriction or an increased RAP may limit benefit. In LVOTO, catecholamine inotropy can be counterproductive. A higher MAP therefore does not establish better tissue flow.

### Bedside application

Choose fluid, a vasopressor, inotropy or obstruction relief according to the mechanism. Evaluate perfusion and measured CO/SV response where indicated, plus lung/venous congestion. Do not use Pmsf as a routine bedside number to chase, and do not interpret a higher CVP after noradrenaline as proof of improved circulating volume.

- For a simplified numerical example, a mean systemic filling pressure of 9 mmHg and right atrial pressure of 5 mmHg give a 4 mmHg driving gradient.
- If venoconstriction increases the upstream pressure to 12 and right atrial pressure rises to 6, the gradient increases to 6 mmHg. If the failing right ventricle instead allows right atrial pressure to rise to 9, the gradient falls to 3 mmHg. These are illustrative values, and flow also depends on resistance.
- At the bedside, a higher MAP with a falling Doppler stroke volume, rising right-sided pressure or worsening refill warrants re-examination of the mechanism before increasing the infusion.

![Return function and cardiac function curves: the working CVP and “return limited” versus “cardiac limited” states](set1-fig-venous.jpg)

[Figure source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3682240/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines stressed versus unstressed volume without treating them as separate anatomical tanks
- Defines Pmsf and the venous-return gradient/resistance relationship
- Distinguishes absolute loss from venodilation/relative underfilling
- Explains noradrenaline's venous recruitment, arterial and cardiac effects
- Explains why afterload/RV dysfunction can prevent CO improvement
- Uses perfusion/flow response and congestion rather than MAP/CVP alone

items.title: 2. A shocked patient has a cardiac output of 3 L/min, haemoglobin 80 g/L and SaO₂…
items.q: A shocked patient has a cardiac output of 3 L/min, haemoglobin 80 g/L and SaO₂ 98%. After treatment the MAP and SaO₂ normalise, but lactate and organ dysfunction persist. Explain oxygen delivery, microcirculatory failure and the pathophysiological consequences of shock, including reperfusion.
items.a:
### Macrovascular oxygen delivery

- Shock is acute circulatory failure with inadequate cellular oxygen delivery **and/or utilisation** relative to metabolic demand.
- Hypotension is common but neither necessary nor sufficient for the diagnosis.
- Arterial oxygen content is approximately **CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hb(g/dL) × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂(mmHg)** in mL O₂/dL.
- Oxygen delivery is **DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ × 10** in mL/min when CO is in L/min.
- Most oxygen is haemoglobin-bound; a normal saturation cannot compensate for severe anaemia or low output.

Here Hb 80 g/L is 8 g/dL. Ignoring the small dissolved component, CaO₂ is approximately **10.5 mL/dL** and DO₂ is **315 mL/min**. If PaO₂ were 100 mmHg, CaO₂ would be about 10.8 and DO₂ about 324 mL/min; PaO₂ was not actually supplied. These are illustrative calculations, not transfusion thresholds. Demand, extraction, disease and regional perfusion determine adequacy.

### Cellular and microcirculatory consequences

- Reduced flow initially increases extraction, but beyond a critical reserve oxygen consumption may become supply-dependent.
- ATP depletion impairs membrane pumps, promoting cell swelling, calcium overload and loss of membrane integrity.
- Lactate can rise from hypoperfusion-related glycolysis, but also adrenergic metabolism and impaired hepatic clearance, so it is not a direct cellular oxygen meter.

- In inflammation/sepsis, endothelial activation, glycocalyx injury and increased permeability cause interstitial oedema.
- Heterogeneous capillary flow, microthrombi, shunting, impaired diffusion/extraction and mitochondrial dysfunction can persist despite a normal MAP/CO.
- Maldistribution means some cells remain underperfused while others receive flow; a high ScvO₂ can coexist with failed extraction.
- A single normal global pressure or saturation therefore does not establish recovery.

### Organ and systemic effects

- **Kidney:** reduced perfusion and venous congestion, inflammatory/tubular injury, oliguria and AKI; urine output can lag and is not a stand-alone fluid target.
- **Brain:** altered mentation and encephalopathy, worsened by sedation, hypoxaemia, glucose or temperature disturbance.
- **Heart:** coronary hypoperfusion and inflammatory myocardial dysfunction can reduce output and worsen the shock spiral; arrhythmia or ischaemia may be both cause and consequence.
- **Lung:** endothelial leak and oedema impair gas exchange; ARDS, excess fluid and cardiac failure can coexist.
- **Gut/liver:** splanchnic hypoperfusion, barrier dysfunction and impaired metabolic/drug/lactate clearance.
- **Coagulation/metabolism:** endothelial-coagulation activation, possible microthrombosis/DIC, acidaemia, temperature disturbance and altered drug handling.

### Reperfusion and clinical application

- Restoring flow is essential, but reperfusion can release potassium, acid/metabolites and inflammatory mediators and generate reactive oxygen species with further membrane/mitochondrial injury.
- Anticipate hypotension, hyperkalaemia and arrhythmia after major reperfusion or tourniquet release, and assess the actual cause rather than describing every postoperative lactate rise as residual hypovolaemia.

- Reassess source/haemorrhage control, output, rhythm, haemoglobin, oxygenation, venous pressure, congestion and regional perfusion.
- Use serial examination, CRT/mentation, gas/lactate trend, organ function and focused imaging; consider flow monitoring when uncertainty changes treatment.
- Treat demonstrable deficits with the appropriate blood/fluid, vasoactive support or relief of obstruction, while avoiding excess afterload or fluid.
- Do not give blood solely to normalise this calculated DO₂, or keep administering fluid until lactate is normal.
- Organ recovery and microcirculatory coherence are the aim, with repeated assessment and acknowledgement that a physiological improvement does not automatically prove a survival benefit. [BJA Education: Vasoactive therapy in shock, 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8212163/) [BJA Education: Fluids in sepsis, 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13366322/) [ESICM circulatory shock and haemodynamic monitoring guideline, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41236566/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines shock including impaired oxygen utilisation
- Calculates CaO₂/DO₂ with correct Hb and volume-unit conversion
- Explains why normal SaO₂/MAP do not establish adequate delivery or extraction
- Describes ATP depletion, endothelial/glycocalyx injury and microvascular heterogeneity
- Links shock to kidney, brain, heart, lung, gut/liver and coagulation dysfunction
- Distinguishes lactate production/clearance from hypoperfusion alone
- Explains reperfusion-related electrolyte, acid and oxidative effects
- Uses integrated serial endpoints without reflex fluid/transfusion targets

items.title: 3. An 82-year-old patient taking a beta-blocker has occult postoperative bleeding.…
items.q: An 82-year-old patient taking a beta-blocker has occult postoperative bleeding. The heart rate is 72/min, BP 110/65 mmHg and initial haemoglobin is unchanged. Explain how you would recognise shock and why these observations may mislead.
items.a:
### Why the observations do not exclude shock

- Blood loss reduces venous return/stroke volume before pressure necessarily falls.
- Sympathetic vasoconstriction and mobilisation of unstressed venous blood may temporarily preserve MAP.
- In an older patient, baseline hypertension may make 110 systolic a substantial relative reduction; reduced cardiac/renal reserve reduces tolerance of loss.
- Beta-blockade can suppress tachycardia, and a pacemaker can fix the rate.
- Initial Hb may remain unchanged when whole blood is lost proportionately, then fall with redistribution or fluid replacement.
- None of these values measures current oxygen delivery.

### Effect of anaesthesia and medication

- Anaesthetic vasodilation/myocardial depression or neuraxial sympathectomy attenuate compensation.
- Sedatives/opioids obscure altered mentation, pain and respiratory responses.
- Mechanical ventilation/PEEP reduces venous return and changes the interpretation of CVP and dynamic indices.
- ACEI/ARB and other vasodilators can magnify hypotension.
- Conversely, vasopressors can restore BP while leaving inadequate flow.
- Shock index is also less reliable with beta-blockade/pacing.

### Recognition and action

- Review baseline/trends, operation, drains, dressings, abdomen and possible concealed bleeding.
- Check CRT, mottling, skin temperature, pulse volume/pulse pressure, alertness when assessable, urine and serial lactate/base deficit.
- Verify all measurements and check airway/circuit if ETCO₂ falls.
- Obtain serial blood gas/Hb, group/crossmatch, coagulation/fibrinogen and calcium; focused echo may help distinguish underfilling, pump dysfunction and obstruction.
- A normal lactate or a small hyperdynamic LV cannot exclude every problem or independently mandate fluid.

- Escalate immediately to surgery/anaesthesia, control haemorrhage and activate the local major-haemorrhage pathway when warranted.
- Replace blood appropriately rather than waiting for Hb to cross a threshold in active major bleeding.
- Titrate perfusion support, keep warm and repeatedly reassess the response.
- Do not transport an unstable patient for diagnostic imaging when urgent haemostasis is required.

- Reassess after each intervention.
- Measure the trajectory of capillary refill, lactate, base deficit, urine output and mental state, and use repeated haemoglobin measurements as the intravascular compartments equilibrate.
- Inspect for bleeding into closed spaces even when drains are empty or blocked.
- A modest fall from a previously hypertensive baseline can be important in an older patient with poor reserve.
- Mobilise surgical review in parallel with resuscitation.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains compensated shock and pressure versus flow
- Explains age/baseline disease and impaired physiological reserve
- Explains beta-blocker/pacemaker effects on HR/shock index
- Explains anaesthesia, sedation, vasodilators and ventilation effects
- Explains why initial Hb can be normal
- Uses serial perfusion signs, relevant labs and focused imaging
- Prioritises haemostasis/blood resuscitation without waiting for a number

items.title: 4. Describe your approach to a patient who is hypotensive and tachycardic in the…
items.q: Describe your approach to a patient who is hypotensive and tachycardic in the operating theatre, and explain how you would classify the shock and use bedside ultrasound to identify the type.
items.a:
### Immediate approach

Call for help, give 100% oxygen, tell the surgeon, check the airway and ventilation, and look at the monitors: ECG rhythm, ETCO2, airway pressure, SpO2 and temperature. Treat anything obvious (arrhythmia, anaphylaxis, bleeding) and support pressure while deciding whether fluid/blood, an inotrope or immediate relief of obstruction is required.

### Classification and what points to each type

- **Hypovolaemic** (haemorrhage, fluid loss): cold, low pulse pressure, falling haemoglobin, possibly small IVC/LV, neither diagnostic by itself; blood in the surgical field, abdomen or drains.
- **Distributive** (sepsis, anaphylaxis, neuraxial block, vasoplegia, drugs): warm periphery, wide pulse pressure, bronchospasm or rash in anaphylaxis, fever or a known source in sepsis; hyperdynamic ventricle.
- **Cardiogenic** (ischaemia, arrhythmia, valve failure, cardiomyopathy): ECG change, raised troponin, pulmonary oedema, dilated poorly contracting ventricle, regional wall motion abnormality.
- **Obstructive** (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, pulmonary embolism, auto-PEEP, caval compression): high CVP or distended neck veins, rising airway pressure, falling ETCO2, dilated right ventricle or pericardial effusion on echo.
- **Mixed** is common (septic cardiomyopathy, bleeding with anaphylaxis).

### Bedside ultrasound (RUSH or similar)

- **1.** **Pump (heart):** left ventricular function, pericardial effusion with right atrial or ventricular collapse, right ventricle larger than left with septal flattening (D sign).
- **2.** **Tank (volume):** IVC size and collapse (limited in ventilated patients)
  - Lung ultrasound for B-lines (interstitial syndrome with several causes)
  - Absent sliding alone is nonspecific, while a true lung point supports pneumothorax but can be absent in a large/tension pneumothorax
  - FAST for free fluid in the abdomen, pleura and pericardium.
- **3.** **Pipes (vessels):** abdominal aorta for aneurysm or dissection flap, and leg veins for DVT.

- Integrate imaging with physiology and previous studies: a small hyperdynamic LV may reflect vasodilatation or low filling, not necessarily a fluid need; poor LV function may be chronic or part of mixed shock.
- RV dilatation can be chronic PH, infarction or acute afterload obstruction and is not proof of PE.
- Free fluid may be ascites rather than blood.
- A negative limited scan does not exclude retroperitoneal bleeding, aortic dissection, PE or loculated tamponade.

### Treatment follows the type

Haemorrhage needs blood and surgical control; anaphylaxis needs adrenaline; sepsis needs fluid, noradrenaline and antibiotics; cardiogenic shock needs inotropes and revascularisation; tension pneumothorax needs decompression; tamponade needs drainage; PE needs oxygen, noradrenaline and thrombolysis or embolectomy.

Arterial line, central access, lactate, blood gas, haemoglobin and cardiac output monitoring guide response. Lactate/base deficit and mottling may support hypoperfusion, but lactate also rises with adrenergic glycolysis and impaired clearance; normal values do not exclude early shock.

### Evidence

Ultrasound-guided assessment improves diagnostic accuracy and treatment speed in undifferentiated shock in observational studies; there is no trial showing improved survival.

### Serial focused questions, not a single diagnostic label

- Ask what intervention the image would change and whether it is technically adequate.
- Compare the heart, lungs and vessels rather than relying on IVC diameter.
- Evaluate LV/RV function, filling, severe valve disease, effusion/tamponade physiology and dynamic LVOTO where trained, plus lungs/pleura, abdominal free fluid and DVT as indicated.
- Repeat after treatment or a clinical change; document limitations and obtain comprehensive echo/TOE, CT or specialist assessment when the focused examination cannot answer the question.
- In immediate life-threatening tension physiology, do not delay decompression for imaging.
- Ultrasound findings inform the circulation phenotype; they do not independently establish a mortality benefit from a resuscitation algorithm. [ESICM circulatory shock and haemodynamic monitoring guideline, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41236566/) [ANZCA Blue Book 2025: lung ultrasound, emergency laparotomy and Sip Til Send](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getcontentasset/d8402efb-afbb-4300-8c72-c86edd93edad/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/2025_blue_book_pdf.pdf?download=1&language=en)

![Focused echocardiography in shock: A–B circumferential pericardial effusion; C–D dilated right ventricle with septal flattening; E dilated left ventricle](set1-fig-echo.jpg)

[Figure source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4331439/)

## Self-marking checklist

- Immediate actions (call for help, oxygen, check monitors)
- Classification into four types with distinguishing signs
- Recognises mixed shock
- Ultrasound approach (pump, tank, pipes)
- Echo findings for each type
- Treatment matched to type
- Monitoring and markers of hypoperfusion

items.title: 5. Discuss how you would decide whether an anaesthetised patient needs more fluid.…
items.q: Discuss how you would decide whether an anaesthetised patient needs more fluid. Describe the dynamic and static indices available, their limitations, and the evidence for goal-directed fluid therapy.
items.a:
### The question

- Fluid responsiveness means that stroke volume rises by 10 to 15% after a defined preload challenge; exact volume, speed and response threshold depend on the test and measurement precision.
- About half of anaesthetised patients are not responsive, and giving fluid to non-responders only adds oedema.
- I therefore use three steps: is there evidence of hypoperfusion, is the patient responsive, and is the risk of fluid acceptable?

### Static indices (poor predictors)

CVP, pulmonary artery occlusion pressure, end-diastolic volume and urine output reflect preload poorly because they depend on compliance, intrathoracic pressure and valve function. An isolated low CVP does not prove hypovolaemia; interpret waveform, trend, RV function and surrounding pressure, and assess venous congestion as well as possible filling.

### Dynamic indices

- **Pulse pressure variation (PPV) and stroke volume variation (SVV):** over 12 to 13% predicts response.
  - They require a closed chest, a sufficiently regular rhythm and controlled ventilation with an adequate cardiopulmonary interaction; conventional thresholds were commonly validated near 8 mL/kg predicted body weight and no right ventricular failure.
  - They are unreliable with low tidal volumes, spontaneous breathing, arrhythmias, open abdomen or high PEEP.
  - A tidal volume challenge (increase to 8 mL/kg for 1 minute) can rescue PPV in lung-protective ventilation.
- **Passive leg raise:** reversible 300 mL autotransfusion; a rise in cardiac output over 10% predicts response.
  - It works in spontaneously breathing patients and arrhythmias, but needs real-time stroke-volume/cardiac-output measurement; operative positioning, abdominal hypertension or inability to reposition may prevent a valid test.
- **Fluid bolus (mini-challenge):** 100 to 250 mL over 1 to 2 minutes, then check stroke volume.
- **End-expiratory occlusion test**, IVC variation on echo, plethysmographic variability index: less well validated.
- **Echo:** LVOT VTI/stroke-volume change during a valid preload test can help. A small hyperdynamic LV or collapsing IVC alone does not establish a need for fluid.

I combine these with lactate, central venous oxygen saturation, capillary refill, mottling and urine output to decide whether the tissues need more flow.

### Goal-directed fluid therapy

- GDT titrates fluid (and sometimes inotropes) to a stroke volume or cardiac output target using oesophageal Doppler, arterial waveform analysis or other devices.
- Early meta-analyses showed fewer complications and shorter hospital stay, but they were small and mostly predated enhanced recovery.
- OPTIMISE (734 high-risk patients) had a non-significant reduction in complications; the updated meta-analysis including it was positive but smaller, and OPTIMISE II (cardiac output-guided fluid) found no benefit with the enhanced-recovery baseline.
- FEDORA found fewer complications with Doppler-guided care in moderate-risk surgery.
- RELIEF (restrictive versus liberal) suggests the baseline fluid rate matters as much as the monitor.

I would use GDT in high-risk major abdominal or vascular surgery, avoid it as a fixed protocol in low-risk surgery, and always combine with a conservative baseline fluid rate.

### Need, response and tolerance

- Demonstrate a reason to augment flow before testing, then ask whether the expected gain outweighs pulmonary/systemic congestion.
- PPV/SVV can be misleading with RV failure, irregular rhythm, spontaneous effort, low driving pressure, open chest or altered abdominal pressure; no single threshold works everywhere.
- Use predicted body weight for a brief tidal-volume challenge and avoid injurious ventilation merely to validate a monitor.
- An end-expiratory occlusion test requires an adequately tolerated pause and sufficiently precise continuous flow measurement.
- OPTIMISE II studied a particular cardiac-output-guided fluid/inotrope algorithm and did not establish routine benefit; it does not mean that monitoring or every targeted intervention is ineffective.
- Goal-directed protocols and monitoring hardware are not interchangeable. [ESICM circulatory shock and haemodynamic monitoring guideline, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41236566/) [OPTIMISE II primary trial, 2024](https://www.bmj.com/content/387/bmj-2024-080439)

![Passive leg raising: five steps for a valid cardiac output response test](set1-fig-plr.jpg)

[Figure source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4293822/)

## Self-marking checklist

- States the aim: identify who will respond to a bolus
- Static indices and why they are poor
- Pulse pressure variation with its limitations
- Passive leg raise and mini-fluid challenge
- Echo and other tools
- Combined with markers of perfusion
- Describes GDT and which patients may benefit
- Evidence summary (OPTIMISE, FEDORA) and its limits

items.title: 6. A postoperative patient has MAP 64 mmHg, high CVP, oliguria, mottled skin and a…
items.q: A postoperative patient has MAP 64 mmHg, high CVP, oliguria, mottled skin and a falling ETCO₂ despite noradrenaline. Discuss how you would distinguish mixed shock, low flow and venous congestion.
items.a:
### Why the pressure is misleading

MAP may have recovered through SVR while **forward CO and effective organ driving pressure remain inadequate**. High CVP may represent RV dysfunction, TR, PEEP, tamponade, intra-abdominal hypertension or fluid accumulation. The kidney depends on both inflow and outflow pressure; a high venous pressure can reduce renal perfusion even with MAP 64.

### Diagnostic priorities

- Check pulse/arterial trace and respiratory circuit; fall in ETCO₂ with controlled ventilation can signal **falling pulmonary blood flow**, but also ventilation/dead-space or sampling changes.
- Assess surgical site/drains for occult bleeding, infection/source control, drugs, rhythm/ECG, airway pressure and PEEP.
- Focused TTE/TOE to examine LV/RV function, pericardial collection, RV pressure/volume load, valve disease, LVOTO, lung B-lines and vena cava. If available, measure CO/SV trend and consider venous Doppler congestion markers in context.
- Use Hb, gas/base deficit, lactate trend, kidney function and ScvO₂ ± CO₂ gap as adjuncts, recognising each can mislead in isolation.

### Management by mechanism

- **Bleeding:** surgical haemostasis and appropriate blood replacement.
- **Vasoplegia:** adequate but not excessive vasopressor to achieve perfusion pressure (noradrenaline ± vasopressin) while reassessing output.
- **Low CO:** treat rhythm/ischaemia and consider selected inotropy if low-flow pump failure is established; avoid escalating afterload without considering SV.
- **Obstruction:** decompress tamponade/tension process and correct high intra-abdominal pressure where appropriate.
- **Venous congestion:** avoid reflex fluid boluses; optimise RV afterload, PEEP and volume; consider decongestion once safe.

### Endpoints

Trend peripheral perfusion, mentation, urine, ETCO₂, CO/SV, lactate, renal function and absence of worsening overload. Reassess diagnosis after each treatment.

- For example, a dilated poorly contracting right ventricle with septal shift suggests that right-sided load is limiting left-sided filling.
- Look for acute embolism, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, excessive PEEP and right ventricular infarction in the appropriate context.
- A small hyperdynamic left ventricle can accompany major blood loss, vasoplegia or left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, so interpret it with the Doppler signal and clinical timing.
- Reassessment should compare the pre-intervention pattern with the response.
- If a pressor restores arterial pressure while refill worsens and measured output falls, reconsider afterload and forward flow before giving more pressor.

Reassess oxygenation and airway pressures during the same review.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises MAP is not CO and high CVP may reduce organ driving pressure
- Checks bleeding, devices, ventilator and causes of changing ETCO₂
- Uses focused ultrasound to discriminate RV/LV failure, obstruction and volume status
- Interprets labs and venous signals in context, not as single-fluid triggers
- Treats bleeding/vasoplegia/low output/obstruction by mechanism
- Avoids automatic fluid boluses in congested patients
- Specifies objective serial perfusion and congestion endpoints

items.title: 7. Falling ETCO₂ and hypotension during laparoscopy
items.q: A patient becomes acutely hypotensive with a falling ETCO2 during laparoscopic surgery. Discuss your approach to the differential diagnosis of obstructive shock.
items.a:
## Obstructive shock

Impaired cardiac output due to **physical obstruction of flow** which may cause secondary RV/LV dysfunction; filling pressures depend on the obstruction and coexisting volume status. Main causes:
- **Pulmonary embolism** (thrombus, air, fat, CO2, amniotic fluid, cement).
- **Tension pneumothorax** (barotrauma, central line, laparoscopic CO2 tracking).
- **Cardiac tamponade**.
- **Auto-PEEP** (dynamic hyperinflation).
- **Aortocaval compression** (pregnancy, pneumoperitoneum).
- Severe **pulmonary hypertension** or right ventricular failure.

## Approach

- **1.** **Recognise** the pattern: hypotension with **fall in ETCO2**, raised CVP/JVP, hypoxaemia, tachycardia.
- **2.** **Immediate steps**: 100% oxygen, **stop insufflation/desufflate**, briefly disconnect the circuit **if severe dynamic hyperinflation is suspected**, allowing passive exhalation, exclude hypovolaemia and anaphylaxis, ask for help.
- **3.** **Look for specific causes**:
  - Tension pneumothorax: unilateral breath sounds, high airway pressures, tracheal shift → **needle or finger decompression, then chest drain**.
  - Gas embolism: sudden ETCO₂ change/collapse and TOE bubbles; a mill-wheel murmur is insensitive. **Stop gas entry/desufflate, stop N₂O, give 100% O₂ and support circulation.** Aspirate via an appropriately positioned **existing** central line if feasible; do not delay resuscitation to insert one. Routine head-down positioning is not recommended, especially with cerebral arterial embolism; consider left lateral/head-down only for a suspected right-heart gas lock when feasible. Urgently discuss hyperbaric treatment for arterial/cerebral embolism or persistent neurological/cardiopulmonary injury.
  - High-risk PE: RV strain supports but does not prove diagnosis. Activate senior PE/cardiothoracic help; UFH and reperfusion selection depend on active bleeding and recent surgery. **Systemic thrombolysis, catheter treatment or surgical embolectomy** are options; surgery/active bleeding can favour mechanical reperfusion. Alteplase 100 mg over 2 h is a recognised adult high-risk PE regimen; arrest dosing varies by protocol—do not present a 50-mg bolus as universal. In arrest, use the current resuscitation algorithm and consider prolonged CPR after thrombolysis.
  - Tamponade: echo.
- **4.** **Point-of-care echo** is the quickest discriminator (RV dilatation, effusion, hypovolaemic collapse).
- **5.** **Haemodynamic support**: noradrenaline, avoid excessive fluid in RV failure, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide), ECMO in refractory cases.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines obstructive shock
- Lists causes
- Recognises the ETCO2 clue
- Immediate manoeuvres
- Cause-specific treatment
- Role of echocardiography
- RV support strategies
- Rescue (thrombolysis, ECMO)

items.title: 8. 'Treating the number' is a criticism of the routine use of vasopressors to…
items.q: 'Treating the number' is a criticism of the routine use of vasopressors to maintain intraoperative blood pressure. Discuss the arguments for and against the routine use of vasoconstrictors to treat intraoperative hypotension, and describe how you would set a blood pressure target for an individual patient.
items.a:
### What pressure tells us—and what it does not

- MAP approximates the product of cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance, with a small contribution from CVP.
- A vasoconstrictor can restore perfusion pressure while cardiac output is unchanged, increased through venous recruitment, or reduced by excess afterload.
- Organ perfusion also depends on venous/compartment pressure, autoregulation, arterial oxygen content and microvascular distribution.
- Thus pressure is necessary information but not a direct measurement of tissue blood flow or oxygen utilisation.

### Arguments for prompt, cause-matched vasopressor treatment

- Anaesthesia and neuraxial blockade frequently cause loss of arterial and venous tone. A titrated pressor can restore pressure and recruit stressed venous volume without an unnecessary fluid load.
- Marked or prolonged hypotension is associated with myocardial injury, AKI and death. Waiting for a slow fluid infusion when vasodilatation is the principal problem can prolong potentially harmful hypotension.
- Septic vasoplegia, anaphylaxis and low-SVR states have specific guideline-supported vasoactive treatment. Adrenaline is essential in anaphylaxis; noradrenaline is first-line in septic shock. Maintaining coronary/RV perfusion can interrupt a low-output spiral.
- A temporary pressor bridge may be necessary during severe haemorrhage while blood and source control are being delivered. It must not mask inadequate replacement or delay control.

### Arguments against a reflex response to every low number

- Check the measurement, transducer level, cuff and arterial waveform. Treating artefact exposes the patient to drug risk.
- Excess vasoconstriction may reduce forward flow, increase LV work or cause regional ischaemia. Phenylephrine often causes reflex bradycardia; noradrenaline is not guaranteed to improve cardiac output.
- Hypotension from haemorrhage, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, severe pump failure or dynamic LVOTO requires a specific intervention. Repeated boluses can temporarily conceal deterioration.

### Set a target and judge the response

- Establish reliable resting/home BP, age, chronic hypertension, coronary/cerebrovascular disease, renal disease, ventricular function, venous pressure and surgical context.
- ACC/AHA 2024 uses MAP ≥60–65/SBP ≥90 as a minimum; AoA/BIHS 2026 describes commonly used MAP >70 and/or SBP >100 targets for higher-risk planned surgery.
- Septic shock generally starts at MAP 65. Trauma with uncontrolled bleeding and raised-ICP or spinal-cord conditions require their own strategy.
- A fixed percentage of a single anxious preoperative reading is not a validated universal goal.

Choose the agent by mechanism:

- Phenylephrine for selected vasodilatation with adequate output and rate.
- Ephedrine for transient vasodilatation/bradycardia.
- Noradrenaline for sustained vasoplegia.
- An inotrope for demonstrated low output when indicated.
- Vasopressin as a selected non-catecholamine adjunct.

- Correct rhythm, depth, oxygenation and volume where relevant.
- Recheck pulse, stroke volume/echo, capillary refill, mentation, urine trend, lactate and congestion.
- None alone proves adequate perfusion; a high lactate is not automatically a request for fluid.

### Evaluate the evidence rather than the slogan

- Walsh's approximately 33,000-patient cohort associated MAP <55 with myocardial/kidney injury, with increasing risk by duration; residual confounding limits causal interpretation.
- Randomised BP strategies have been studied.
- INPRESS suggested benefit from an individualised SBP strategy in selected high-risk surgery, whereas **IMPROVE-multi (2025)** did not reduce its early organ-injury/death composite using preoperative nighttime MAP targets compared with routine MAP ≥65.
- This does not prove that hypotension is harmless or that all individualisation fails.
- It argues against declaring a single target/pressor strategy universally outcome-improving.
- My practice is timely treatment of clinically significant hypotension, followed by confirmation that pressure restoration improved the circulation. [AoA/BIHS 2026 perioperative BP guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41532177/) [IMPROVE-multi primary trial, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41076588/) [BJA Education: Vasoactive therapy in shock, 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8212163/) [ANZCA Blue Book archive: 2023 vasoconstrictor perspective](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/advocacy/college-publications/australasian-anaesthesia-(the-blue-book))

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains pressure versus flow, venous pressure and oxygen delivery
- Identifies legitimate cause-specific pressor indications
- Discusses afterload, bradycardia, ischaemia, access and dosing harms
- Corrects the assumption that all LV outflow obstruction is worsened by pressors
- Sets a named-guideline, context-specific pressure goal
- Assesses perfusion and fluid need/response/tolerance beyond MAP
- Critically compares observational evidence with randomised target trials
- Distinguishes the Blue Book perspective from contemporary consensus

items.title: 9. Discuss the principles of anaesthetic induction and maintenance in a patient…
items.q: Discuss the principles of anaesthetic induction and maintenance in a patient who is in hypovolaemic or septic shock and requires emergency surgery. Which drugs would you choose and which would you avoid?
items.a:
### Principles

- A shocked patient has maximal sympathetic tone supporting their pressure.
- Induction drugs remove it, positive pressure ventilation reduces venous return, and low output may prolong arm–brain circulation time, delaying apparent onset; reduced central distribution and sensitivity can then produce an exaggerated effect.
- Avoid rapidly stacking additional doses before the first has arrived.
- The plan is therefore to resuscitate first, reduce the dose, and be ready for arrest.

- **1.** **Resuscitate before induction** if surgery allows: blood or fluid, vasopressor started (noradrenaline infusion or boluses of metaraminol, phenylephrine or ephedrine), arterial line placed under local anaesthetic.
- **2.** **Prepare:** surgeon scrubbed and ready, adrenaline drawn up, defibrillator, two experienced anaesthetists, pre-oxygenation with high-flow nasal oxygen, and a plan for a difficult airway.
- **3.** **Position and monitoring:** head-up ramped position, arterial line, ECG, SpO2, ETCO2, and a defibrillator.

### Drug choice

- **Induction agent:** ketamine 0.5 to 1 mg/kg is my first choice (sympathomimetic effect; direct myocardial depression in catecholamine-depleted patients).
  - Etomidate 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg preserves haemodynamics but causes adrenal suppression after a single dose, which matters in septic shock, but routine hydrocortisone solely because etomidate was given is not recommended; treat the actual septic-shock/steroid indication.
  - Propofol and thiopentone should be avoided or reduced to a fraction (0.25 to 0.5 mg/kg), since they cause vasodilatation and myocardial depression.
- **Opioid:** fentanyl 1 to 2 micrograms/kg or remifentanil titrated, which can blunt laryngoscopy but may remove sympathetic support, cause bradycardia and worsen hypotension; substantially reduce/omit a bolus when appropriate and titrate.
- **Neuromuscular blocker:** rocuronium 1 to 1.2 mg/kg for rapid sequence induction, with sugammadex available. Suxamethonium is an alternative if no contraindication (hyperkalaemia, burns, prolonged immobilisation).
- **Maintenance:** low-dose volatile (0.3 to 0.5 MAC) or total intravenous anaesthesia titrated to processed EEG, with neuromuscular blockade and opioid. Avoid awareness: accept amnestic doses even if hypotensive, and add ketamine or midazolam if the patient cannot tolerate volatile.
- **Avoid:** large boluses of propofol, nitrous oxide in bowel obstruction, high-dose volatile, epidural or spinal anaesthesia in uncorrected hypovolaemia or coagulopathy.

### Ventilation and ongoing care

Use low tidal volume (6 to 8 mL/kg) and the lowest PEEP that maintains oxygenation, as high intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return. Expect hypotension on starting ventilation. Give calcium, correct acidosis only if severe, and warm the patient. After surgery continue in ICU with sedation and ventilation.

### Evidence

Etomidate causes adrenal suppression after a single dose, but trials comparing it with ketamine show no consistent mortality difference. Etomidate-associated adrenal suppression does not establish benefit from automatic steroid cover after a single dose.

### Make the transition survivable

- Agree the earliest safe incision and the time available for stabilisation.
- A vasopressor should be connected, primed and running when needed, not merely prescribed.
- Preoxygenation strategy and position must balance oxygen reserve against venous return; consider ramping in obesity without worsening shock.
- Protect against aspiration with an appropriate rapid-sequence plan, suction and a trained rescue team.
- Neither ketamine nor etomidate guarantees haemodynamic stability, and an arbitrary 0.3–0.5 MAC must not become a ceiling that causes awareness.
- Titrate hypnosis, analgesia and ventilation using clinical/EEG information and perfusion; avoid excessive mean airway pressure while maintaining adequate oxygenation.
- Reassess immediately after intubation because PPV, occult auto-PEEP, anaesthetic effects and the disease can all worsen output. [BJA Education: Vasoactive therapy in shock, 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8212163/) [ANZCA Blue Book 2025: lung ultrasound, emergency laparotomy and Sip Til Send](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getcontentasset/d8402efb-afbb-4300-8c72-c86edd93edad/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/2025_blue_book_pdf.pdf?download=1&language=en)

## Self-marking checklist

- Resuscitation before induction
- Preparation (vasopressor ready, arterial line, team)
- Reduced-dose induction agent with justification
- Ketamine and etomidate points
- Avoiding propofol or thiopentone boluses
- Rocuronium and rapid sequence plan
- Maintenance strategy and awareness
- Ventilation settings and effect on venous return
- Postoperative ICU care

items.title: 10. After cardiac surgery an ICU team proposes concentrated albumin to prevent…
items.q: After cardiac surgery an ICU team proposes concentrated albumin to prevent acute kidney injury. Evaluate this proposal and explain how fluid choice differs from routine volume replacement.
items.a:
### Comparison

- **Distribution:** crystalloid distributes in the extracellular compartment, but intravascular retention depends on time, infusion rate and physiology. Albumin retention also varies; it is not an impermeable intravascular reservoir.
- **Volume needed:** fixed 3:1 crystalloid/blood or 1:1 colloid replacement rules are unreliable and risk overload; give measured aliquots to a defined goal.
- **Effect:** colloid gives a larger, longer rise in preload; crystalloid more oedema.
- **Safety:** saline causes hyperchloraemic acidosis; balanced solutions reduce hyperchloraemia, but a universal mortality advantage over saline has not been established.
  - Starches cause AKI, RRT, coagulopathy and death; gelatins cause anaphylaxis; albumin has indication-specific harms and substantial cost; neither a low serum level nor capillary leak alone establishes benefit.

The revised Starling model explains the difference in effect: the endothelial barrier and subglycocalyx oncotic gradient govern transcapillary exchange; lymphatic return is central and sustained venous-end reabsorption is limited. In sepsis, trauma and major surgery the glycocalyx is damaged, so colloid leaks too, and the advantage shrinks.

### Choice for the hypovolaemic patient

First treat the cause. If he is bleeding, the answer is blood, not either fluid. For hypovolaemia from fasting, vomiting or vasodilatation, I choose a balanced crystalloid (Plasma-Lyte or Hartmann's) 250 to 500 mL boluses guided by dynamic indices, with reassessment after each bolus. The reasons are:

- Colloids have not reduced mortality in resuscitation trials (SAFE, CRISTAL, ALBIOS) and cost far more.
- Hydroxyethyl starch is contraindicated in sepsis and critical illness (6S, CHEST) after renal harm in critical-care trials and increased mortality in the 6S severe-sepsis trial; CHEST did not show a statistically significant overall mortality difference; the regulators have withdrawn or restricted it.
- Gelatin carries a risk of anaphylaxis and has no outcome data.
- Balanced crystalloid reduced major adverse kidney events compared with saline in critically ill patients (SMART), though SPLIT, BaSICS and PLUS showed no clear mortality difference.

I would consider albumin selectively after substantial crystalloid with an ongoing volume indication, rather than treating hypoalbuminaemia alone, in cirrhosis with paracentesis or SBP (20% albumin), or when sodium load must be limited. In traumatic brain injury I avoid albumin (worse outcomes in the SAFE subgroup) and prefer saline over slightly hypotonic Hartmann's.

Avoid both if the patient is euvolaemic: a fixed maintenance rate of 1 to 2 mL/kg/hour is enough for most elective surgery.

### Evidence

- SAFE (about 7000 ICU patients): albumin 4% and saline had similar mortality, with a signal of harm in TBI.
- 6S showed increased death/RRT with starch in severe sepsis; CHEST showed increased RRT without a significant mortality difference.
- CRISTAL: no 28-day mortality difference, with an exploratory 90-day benefit for colloid.
- SMART: fewer major adverse kidney events with balanced crystalloids.

### Current interpretation and endpoints

- SSC 2026 favours crystalloids alone over routine supplemental albumin, allowing selected exceptions after large crystalloid volumes or in cirrhosis.
- Distinguish 4% resuscitation albumin from a postoperative 20% infusion: ALBICS-AKI (2025) did not show renal protection in high-risk cardiac surgery and found an increased adjusted AKI risk.
- This does not prove identical harm for every albumin concentration or indication, but contradicts an unqualified “no renal signal” claim.

- ALBICS-AKI evaluated postoperative 20% albumin in cardiac surgical patients at increased renal risk.
- It did not establish renal protection and reported a higher risk of AKI with the albumin strategy.
- This differs from the 4% albumin comparison during and after bypass in ALBICS.
- Apply the evidence to the proposed prophylactic indication, then treat an actual fluid deficit according to perfusion, congestion and the cause of the deficit.

## Self-marking checklist

- Direct comparison of distribution, volume required and effect
- Safety profiles of each colloid
- Glycocalyx and revised Starling explanation
- Treat the cause; blood if bleeding
- Chooses balanced crystalloid with justification
- States when albumin is appropriate
- Contraindications (starch in sepsis, albumin in TBI)
- Dynamic assessment and avoiding overload
- Evidence briefly

items.title: 11. Discuss restrictive versus liberal perioperative fluid therapy for a…
items.q: Discuss restrictive versus liberal perioperative fluid therapy for a 68-year-old undergoing elective major abdominal surgery. How would you plan fluid management from the preoperative period to the day after surgery?
items.a:
### Restrictive versus liberal

- Liberal regimens (10 to 12 mL/kg/hour or a net positive balance over 3 to 7 L) replace third-space losses and cause weight gain, bowel oedema, impaired anastomotic healing, pulmonary complications, ileus and prolonged stay.
- Restrictive regimens (about 1 to 4 mL/kg/hour crystalloid with no third-space replacement) were thought to reduce those but risk hypovolaemia and AKI.
- RELIEF (3000 patients) compared them and found no difference in disability-free survival, with a higher AKI rate and more renal replacement therapy with the restrictive arm.
- The present consensus is a "zero-balance" or near-euvolaemic approach, individualised with monitoring.

### Plan

**Before surgery**

- Do not fast for long: clear fluids until 2 hours before surgery, and carbohydrate drinks in ERAS pathways.
- Use the surgery-specific bowel-preparation/antibiotic pathway; if preparation is indicated, assess and replace actual deficits rather than assuming a routine IV requirement.
- Treat the patient's baseline: renal function, heart failure and medications (diuretics, ACE inhibitors).

**During surgery**

- Maintenance balanced crystalloid 1 to 3 mL/kg/hour as an example only, individualised to size, duration, disease and measured losses rather than claimed as the RELIEF trial prescription, with no routine third-space replacement.
- Replace measured losses: blood volume for blood, with blood according to active bleeding, perfusion and a context-specific transfusion threshold; Hb 70–80 g/L is not a trigger rule for uncontrolled haemorrhage or every cardiac condition.
- Treat hypotension with a vasopressor first when the patient is not hypovolaemic, rather than repeated boluses.
- Use dynamic indices or a cardiac output monitor to guide boluses of 250 mL in high-risk patients.
- Use an arterial line and urine output as a trend, not a target (0.5 mL/kg/hour is often not meaningful under anaesthesia).
- Prevent hypothermia, use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, and use regional or epidural techniques with careful vasopressor management.

**After surgery**

- Early oral intake and stopping IV fluids when drinking, usually within 24 hours.
- Monitor weight, balance, urine output, creatinine and sodium; give maintenance only if oral intake is inadequate.
- Treat low urine output with assessment (volume, obstruction, pain), not a reflex bolus.

### Evidence

- The restrictive approach was supported by Brandstrup (2003, colorectal surgery, fewer complications), but the restrictive arm used much less fluid than modern regimens.
- RELIEF showed no benefit and more AKI.
- Meta-analyses of GDT favour individualised therapy.
- Enhanced-recovery care aims at euvolaemia and avoiding both excess and under-resuscitation; evidence for a specific GDT algorithm must be considered separately.

### Avoid turning an evidence label into a prescription

- RELIEF compared two defined perioperative regimens, not every possible “restrictive” and “liberal” practice.
- It found more AKI without improved disability-free survival in the restrictive group, so an obligatory zero or negative balance is not the objective for a patient who is still losing fluid.
- A 1–3 mL/kg/h rate is only a possible basal starting point; it does not replace blood, measured gastrointestinal losses or an evidenced resuscitation need.
- Conversely, a fasting history alone does not justify fixed large deficit/third-space replacement.
- Use the local clear-fluid policy only in eligible elective patients, not bowel obstruction or high aspiration risk.
- Specify stop/review criteria for postoperative IV fluids and assess venous congestion or obstruction before treating oliguria with more fluid. [RELIEF primary trial, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1801601) [ANZCA Blue Book 2025: lung ultrasound, emergency laparotomy and Sip Til Send](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getcontentasset/d8402efb-afbb-4300-8c72-c86edd93edad/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/2025_blue_book_pdf.pdf?download=1&language=en)

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines restrictive and liberal regimens with harms of each
- RELIEF result and the consensus on near-zero balance
- Preoperative fasting and carbohydrate
- Intraoperative rate with no third-space replacement
- Blood replaced with blood and haemoglobin triggers
- Vasopressor use instead of repeated boluses
- Dynamic indices or cardiac output monitoring in high-risk patients
- Postoperative early oral intake and monitoring
- Avoids reflex boluses for low urine output

items.title: 12. Balanced crystalloid, saline and colloid in hypovolaemic shock
items.q: Compare the use of balanced crystalloids, 0.9% saline and synthetic colloids in the resuscitation of a patient with hypovolaemic shock.
items.a:
## Properties

- **0.9% saline**: Na and Cl 154 mmol/L each, strong ion difference zero; large volumes cause **hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis**. The chloride load, rather than bag pH, explains this. Kidney effects vary by population/trial; avoid claiming universal AKI harm. Useful for **chloride-depletion alkalosis**; commonly preferred for initial isotonic resuscitation in **TBI**. Hypertonic therapy for intracranial hypertension is a separate indication.
- **Balanced crystalloids** (Hartmann's/lactated Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte): closer to plasma, with buffers (lactate, acetate, gluconate). Hartmann's is slightly hypotonic (not ideal for TBI); Plasma-Lyte is isotonic. Potassium content (4–5 mmol/L) does not automatically contraindicate use in renal impairment; still consider measured K, excretory function and acid–base status. Isotonicity alone does not establish the best fluid for TBI.
- **Synthetic colloids** (hydroxyethyl starch, gelatin): may provide greater initial plasma expansion per volume; capillary leak limits retention and no reliable universal crystalloid:colloid replacement ratio applies. Each has toxicity.

## Evidence

- **SPLIT, SMART, PLUS**: balanced crystalloids reduced major adverse kidney events in some (SMART), though effects on mortality were small or absent (PLUS).
- **Starches:** **CHEST** increased RRT use without a statistically significant mortality difference; **6S** found increased mortality and RRT in severe sepsis. CRYSTMAS is not interchangeable proof of either outcome. Avoid HES in critically ill/septic patients.
- **Gelatin**: anaphylaxis risk, coagulopathy.
- **SAFE**: albumin was equivalent to saline overall.
- **Resuscitation of haemorrhage**: blood is the preferred replacement; large crystalloid volumes cause dilution, coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia.

## Conclusion

Use **balanced crystalloid** first, in measured boluses with reassessment; **saline** for specific indications; **avoid starches**; use **blood products** early for haemorrhage.

> **Evidence anchor:** Fluids in sepsis (2026); CHEST; current SSC guidance. See the source section for review depth and links.

## Self-marking checklist

- Composition and acid–base effects of saline versus balanced fluid
- Appropriate fluid for TBI and hypochloraemia
- Colloid properties and rationale
- Starch harm evidence (CHEST, 6S)
- Balanced fluid trial evidence
- Gelatin and albumin points
- Role of blood in haemorrhage
- A reasoned conclusion

items.title: 13. A 62-year-old patient with bowel obstruction has had 1.5 L/day of nasogastric…
items.q: A 62-year-old patient with bowel obstruction has had 1.5 L/day of nasogastric losses, is tachycardic and oliguric, and has hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Discuss perioperative resuscitation, maintenance and ongoing-loss replacement.
items.a:
### Physiological diagnosis

Persistent vomiting/NG suction causes **loss of water, sodium, chloride, gastric HCl and often potassium**. This produces extracellular volume depletion with **hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis**, secondary K loss and potentially AKI. Hypotension and oliguria may reflect poor forward flow, but interpretation needs serial clinical examination.

### Initial assessment and resuscitation

- ABCDE, actual BP/pulse waveform, perfusion (CRT, mental state, urine), focused loss history, abdominal examination and possible sepsis/ischaemia.
- Establish IV access; measure blood gas, K, Cl, Na, Mg, glucose, creatinine, lactate and Hb; ECG if hypokalaemia.
- If hypoperfused, give a **small 250–500 mL isotonic crystalloid aliquot** (less if limited cardiac reserve), then reassess SV/MAP, CRT, respiratory signs and congestion; repeat only if beneficial and safe.
- Initial perfusion resuscitation can use balanced fluid, but **0.9% saline may be specifically useful to replace sustained gastric chloride loss**, with separate carefully prescribed K replacement. Avoid treating chloride-depletion alkalosis with endless chloride-poor fluid.

### Write three prescriptions, not one

- **1.** **Resuscitation:** short-term aliquots for current hypoperfusion with a stated response endpoint.
- **2.** **Maintenance:** actual daily water, sodium, potassium and glucose requirements, subtracting oral/enteral intake and medication-infusion volumes and adjusting for renal function.
- **3.** **Ongoing measured losses:** replace NG aspirate according to **measured volume and electrolyte pattern**, reassessing frequent electrolytes and acid–base; never add K indiscriminately in oliguria.

### Anaesthesia and surgery

- Elective procedures: correct major dehydration, AKI and dangerous K disturbances first. For suspected strangulation/ischaemia, **resuscitate concurrently with urgent surgery**.
- Anticipate aspiration, haemodynamic collapse at induction and worsened venous return with positive pressure; decompress stomach, plan airway, monitor and have vasoactives prepared.
- Reassess after surgery for ongoing NG losses, infection and fluid overload.

- For example, 1.5 L measured over 24 hours averages about 63 mL/h, but the prescription should track the actual recent aspirate and serial chemistry.
- Correct magnesium when low because deficiency can perpetuate potassium loss.
- Confirm urine output and renal function before routine potassium addition and follow the local monitored replacement protocol.
- Check the trend in chloride, bicarbonate and potassium before using a fixed prescription for the next shift.

Document the review time, target urine trend and the triggers to call for senior review.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains chloride/HCl and volume losses causing alkalosis and K depletion
- Assesses perfusion, organ injury and electrolytes before fluids
- Uses titrated isotonic resuscitation with a specified reassessment endpoint
- Distinguishes resuscitation, maintenance and ongoing-loss prescriptions
- Recognises when chloride-rich saline and monitored K replacement are appropriate
- Individualises operative timing to source control and physiological stability
- Mentions aspiration, induction risk and postoperative monitoring

items.title: 14. A 4-year-old, 16 kg, is scheduled for emergency appendicectomy for perforated…
items.q: A 4-year-old, 16 kg, is scheduled for emergency appendicectomy for perforated appendicitis. She has been vomiting for two days. Discuss your fluid management and explain why the choice of fluid matters in children.
items.a:
### Assessment of her deficit
