## Self-marking checklist

- Mechanisms (sympathetic block, cardiac accelerators, Bezold–Jarisch, hypovolaemia)
- Why the elderly are vulnerable
- Immediate treatment with drug choice by heart rate
- Fluid strategy
- Exclusion of other causes
- Technique to reduce risk (dose, baricity, positioning)
- Prophylactic vasopressor infusion
- Monitoring and evidence briefly (REGAIN)

items.title: 2016.1 Q14: Hypertension in PACU after sleeve gastrectomy
items.q: An obese 55-year-old female has undergone sleeve gastrectomy which concluded one hour earlier. The post anaesthetic care unit has called to report a blood pressure of 190/110 mmHg. Discuss your approach to the evaluation and management of the hypertension.
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** original report checked. A passing answer needed a reasonable differential with at least three plausible causes, treatment of common causes and a chosen drug regimen. The task is postoperative hypertension, not a general essay about essential hypertension.

### Evaluate urgency and confirm the reading

- Attend promptly.
- Check ABC, alertness, ventilation, SpO₂, HR/rhythm and the BP trend against the preoperative baseline.
- Repeat with an appropriately sized cuff—particularly important in obesity—or verify the arterial trace.
- Look for chest pain/ECG ischaemia, pulmonary oedema, neurological change, surgical bleeding and other acute hypertension-mediated organ injury.
- A single 190/110 reading without injury is not itself a hypertensive emergency.

### Differential in this patient

- Common causes include pain, anxiety/agitation, hypoxaemia or hypercapnia (OSA, airway obstruction, opioid-related hypoventilation), nausea, shivering/hypothermia and urinary retention.
- Review missed antihypertensives/withdrawal, drugs or residual stimulation, fluid excess and chronic uncontrolled BP.
- Consider less common causes only when supported by the presentation; neurological deterioration may require urgent brain imaging.
- Examine the abdomen, wounds and drains, and consider surgical complications rather than assuming all agitation is pain.

### Treat the cause and titrate BP treatment

- Correct airway obstruction/ventilation, give appropriate oxygen and monitored analgesia without worsening sedation, treat nausea/shivering and relieve retention.
- If hypertension remains sustained and clinically important, use a short-acting titratable agent selected for physiology.
- For a tachycardic patient without bronchospasm, bradycardia/heart block or low-output failure, a **labetalol 5–10 mg IV starting bolus**, reassessed and repeated per local policy, is a reasonable perioperative example.
- A titrated nicardipine infusion is an alternative; nitrates suit myocardial ischaemia or hypertensive pulmonary oedema when not contraindicated.

- Avoid an abrupt fall to an arbitrary normal value.
- With a true hypertensive emergency use monitored, organ-specific treatment; many presentations use an initial MAP reduction no greater than about 20–25% in the first hour, but aortic, obstetric and neurological conditions have different pathways.
- Escalate to senior anaesthesia/ICU if organ injury, refractory BP or respiratory support is required.

### Follow-up

Repeat BP/perfusion/ventilation assessments after every intervention. Plan recovery disposition, appropriate chronic-drug restart and handover/GP follow-up for persistent hypertension.

Obesity makes an undersized cuff a plausible source of error, and a satisfactory saturation on supplemental oxygen can conceal hypoventilation. Look for obstructed breathing and rising carbon dioxide before escalating opioid analgesia. Severe BP plus new chest pain, pulmonary oedema, a focal deficit or altered consciousness changes the urgency and the investigation pathway.
rubric: Confirms measurement, cuff size and baseline/trend
Checks airway/ventilation/OSA, oxygenation and acute organ injury
Gives at least three likely PACU causes with patient-specific reasoning
Treats reversible causes before repeated antihypertensive dosing
Chooses an appropriate titratable drug with dose and contraindications
Avoids precipitous BP reduction and distinguishes emergency from a high number
Includes escalation, repeat assessment, handover and follow-up

items.title: 2015.1 Q4: Septic shock: resuscitation goals and ongoing fluid options
items.q: A 40-year-old 100 kg patient presents with septicaemia of unknown cause. After receiving two litres of 0.9% NaCl (Normal Saline) as initial resuscitation the patient has the following observations: HR 126 bpm; BP 80/40 mmHg. Outline your initial resuscitation goals. (30%) Evaluate options for ongoing fluid resuscitation at this time. (70%)
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** original report checked. State at least three goals, then evaluate crystalloids versus colloids rather than spending the whole answer on a sepsis bundle. Contemporary guidance qualifies the historical answer.

### Resuscitation goals (30%)

- Restore effective circulation and tissue perfusion while identifying/treating the infection.
- Initial goals include an individualised MAP (commonly **65 mmHg** initially), improving CRT/mentation, adequate oxygenation and serial improvement in lactate/base deficit; urine output around **0.5 mL/kg/h** is a contextual, delayed endpoint.
- Assess cardiac output and congestion when the response is unclear.
- Do not force every endpoint to normal with fluid alone.
- Obtain cultures without delaying antimicrobials and arrange prompt source assessment/control.

### Evaluate further fluid (70%)

- The observed BP implies MAP about 53 mmHg and serious instability.
- Confirm the signal, assess perfusion, losses, cardiac function and pulmonary/venous congestion; treat while assessing.
- The 2 L already given is **20 mL/kg using the stated 100 kg**, but weight alone does not establish obesity or an appropriate final volume.
- The 2026 SSC suggests ≥30 mL/kg initial crystalloid within 3 h with frequent individualised reassessment; this is not an instruction to give the next litre without considering benefit/tolerance.
- In unstable shock, start **noradrenaline concurrently** through suitable monitored peripheral access while arranging definitive access if indicated.

- **Balanced isotonic crystalloid:** reasonable default for further resuscitation.
  - Give a monitored aliquot (e.g. 250–500 mL, smaller with limited reserve), reassess forward SV/CO where feasible, CRT/MAP and congestion, and repeat only while beneficial.
  - It reduces chloride exposure compared with further saline, although large trials do not establish a universal mortality advantage.
- **0.9% saline:** available and effective for extracellular-volume replacement, but additional large volumes increase chloride load/hyperchloraemic acidosis. It remains useful in specific settings such as chloride depletion or TBI; neither is described here.
- **Albumin:** potentially less administered volume, but capillary leak reduces retention; expense, overload and lack of an overall survival benefit matter. SAFE/ALBIOS do not justify routine superiority. Selected supplemental use after large crystalloid volumes/cirrhosis differs from routine first-line use; avoid in TBI.
- **HES/gelatin:** avoid HES in sepsis because of renal and outcome harms. Gelatin has uncertain benefit with anaphylaxis/coagulation concerns and is discouraged by current SSC guidance.
- **Blood:** appropriate for significant haemorrhage or a specific transfusion indication, not routine volume expansion in non-bleeding sepsis. Do not pursue a high Hb solely to satisfy historical EGDT.

Use a valid dynamic test when deciding ongoing fluid, and separate **need, responsiveness and tolerance**. If flow/perfusion fail to improve, reconsider vasoplegia, myocardial dysfunction, obstruction or an uncontrolled source. Stop fluid if ineffective or harmful; write maintenance/loss replacement separately.

items.title: 2015.1 Q3: Pericardial effusion six weeks after cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient who is 6 weeks post cardiac surgery has a pericardial effusion requiring treatment. Outline the symptoms and signs of this condition. (70%) Which of these features would trigger an urgent intervention? (30%)
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** original report checked. Show the range from an asymptomatic/slowly developing effusion to acute severe tamponade. **Do not assume that every effusion is tamponade.**

### Symptoms and signs (70%)

- A slow-growing effusion may be asymptomatic; symptoms depend on rate of accumulation and haemodynamic effect, not simply size.
- Ask about progressive dyspnoea, reduced exercise tolerance, orthopnoea, fatigue, chest discomfort, dizziness/presyncope and reduced urine.
- An inflammatory post-pericardiotomy syndrome may include pleuritic pain or fever; anticoagulation/bleeding are relevant to delayed haemopericardium.

- Look for tachycardia, raised JVP, narrow pulse pressure, hypotension, pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory fall in systolic BP during spontaneous breathing), cool peripheries, delayed CRT, altered mentation and oliguria.
- Heart sounds can be muffled, but **Beck's triad is insensitive**; JVP may not be high with coexisting hypovolaemia.
- A pericardial rub suggests inflammation rather than establishing tamponade.

- Investigations support recognition: ECG may show low voltage/electrical alternans; CXR may show an enlarged globular silhouette in a sufficiently large/chronic effusion but can be normal.
- **Echo** assesses size, distribution and haemodynamic effect—RA collapse during ventricular systole, RV collapse in early diastole, a plethoric IVC and respiratory filling changes may support tamponade.
- Loculated postoperative collections, high right-heart pressures and positive-pressure ventilation can obscure classic signs.
- Use TOE or expert imaging if TTE is inadequate; do not delay decompression in cardiovascular collapse.

### Features requiring urgent action (30%)

- Haemodynamic instability or deteriorating organ perfusion consistent with tamponade requires **urgent drainage/surgical review:** progressive hypotension, rising pressor need, syncope/altered mentation, worsening oliguria, marked tachycardia or peri-arrest/arrest.
- Rapid progression and convincing echo evidence of chamber compression strengthen urgency.
- Severe breathlessness/orthopnoea, ongoing bleeding or rapidly accumulating effusion also demand immediate specialist assessment.

- A stable effusion without haemodynamic compromise does not automatically require emergency drainage just because it is large.
- In the unstable postoperative patient, loculated clot/ongoing bleeding often favours surgery; accessible non-clotted fluid may suit image-guided percutaneous drainage.
- The question principally asks **recognition and urgency**, not a long procedural description.

- The late postoperative setting raises the possibility of loculated fluid compressing a single chamber.
- A standard transthoracic window can miss this.
- If the patient is deteriorating and bedside findings remain suspicious, escalate to the cardiac surgical team and arrange suitable expert imaging without delaying definitive treatment.
- A small, rapidly accumulating collection can be more dangerous than a large chronic one.

![Tamponade: haemodynamic changes with increasing pericardial volume (a) and the pericardial pressure–volume relationship for rapid versus slow effusion (b)](set1-fig-tamponade.jpg)

[Figure source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808091/)

Lists breathlessness/orthopnoea and systemic low-output symptoms
Explains tamponade signs and the limitations of Beck's triad/pulsus paradoxus
Describes supportive ECG/CXR and relevant echo signs with postoperative caveats
Recognises shock/deteriorating perfusion as the urgent drainage trigger
Distinguishes effusion size from haemodynamic tamponade
Matches answer emphasis to the 70/30 weighting

items.title: 2011.1 Q4: Human albumin for perioperative volume replacement
items.q: Evaluate the use of human albumin in perioperative volume replacement.
items.model:
> **Examiner report verified:** 2011.1 Q4, pass rate 11%. The report requires properties, advantages/disadvantages, critical evaluation of evidence including SAFE/meta-analyses, and perioperative context. It is not an official model answer. Contemporary evidence is distinguished below.

### Properties and role

- Human albumin is a **plasma-derived colloid** (4–5% approximately iso-oncotic or 20–25% concentrated/hyperoncotic), molecular mass ~66 kDa and a major contributor to plasma oncotic pressure.
- It binds endogenous substances and drugs and has non-oncotic biological functions.
- Its immediate plasma-expanding effect depends on **endothelial permeability, vascular tone and the underlying illness:** retention is **unpredictable in capillary leak**.
- Hyperoncotic albumin may expand plasma volume, but sustained interstitial reabsorption is limited under the revised Starling model; neither oedema mobilisation nor improved tissue perfusion is guaranteed.

### Advantages

- May provide greater **intravascular expansion per administered volume** than crystalloid in selected conditions, although this advantage varies with capillary permeability.
- Avoids the established renal/coagulation harms associated with **hydroxyethyl starch** in critically ill patients; infusion reactions are still possible.
- Has established **specific cirrhosis-related indications**, particularly after large-volume paracentesis and certain complications, according to relevant protocols.

### Disadvantages

- **Cost** and limited supply; pooled human product (small theoretical infection or prion risk).
- No demonstrated overall survival advantage over appropriate crystalloid in most general resuscitation populations; **fluid overload/pulmonary oedema** are still possible.
- Hyperoncotic formulations may redistribute fluid and require monitoring; acute TBI is an important harm signal. Product choice must take renal/cardiac function, sodium content, patient preference and availability into account.

### Evidence (and its quality)

- **SAFE** (~7000 ICU patients, 4% albumin versus saline): no overall mortality advantage; secondary TBI analyses found harm with albumin. The severe-sepsis subgroup signal is not proof of benefit. Extrapolation from ICU to perioperative care is imperfect.
- **ALBIOS** (20% albumin in severe sepsis): no overall mortality benefit; subgroup findings are uncertain.
- Systematic reviews have not established a general survival advantage for albumin over crystalloids. **2026 SSC** conditionally favours crystalloids alone over routine supplemental albumin in sepsis/shock, while permitting selected use after large crystalloid volumes or with cirrhosis.
- **Large-volume paracentesis** has a specific evidence-based indication. Do not present cardiac-surgery circuit priming or perioperative hypoalbuminaemia as proof of a universal albumin outcome benefit.

### Perioperative settings

- **Haemorrhage/obstetrics/trauma:** haemostasis and appropriate blood components restore oxygen carriage and haemostasis; albumin does not replace either function.
- **Liver disease/transplantation:** distinguish specific cirrhosis indications from routine replacement during an operation. Hypoalbuminaemia alone does not establish benefit from correction.

### Conclusion

Albumin is an **expensive, selectively useful colloid**, not a universally effective or risk-free volume expander. Use **appropriate crystalloid first** for most non-haemorrhagic volume resuscitation; reserve albumin for evidence-supported indications or individually justified cases, while accounting for capillary leak/overload and **avoiding it in TBI**.

### Distinguish modern trials and indications

- **ALBICS (2022)** compared 4% albumin with Ringer acetate during/on the first postoperative day of on-pump cardiac surgery: it did not reduce major adverse events and increased bleeding/transfusion-related outcomes.
- **ALBICS-AKI (2025)** tested postoperative **20%** albumin in 611 high-risk cardiac-surgery patients in its primary analysis; it did not confer renal protection and found an increased adjusted AKI risk.
- Do not conflate the regimens, populations or endpoints, or claim albumin has no renal/coagulation safety signal in every setting. [ALBICS 4% albumin primary trial, 2022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35852528/) [ALBICS-AKI 20% albumin primary trial, 2025](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamasurgery/fullarticle/2835041)

- **ATTIRE** did not improve its infection/renal-dysfunction/death composite by targeting albumin ≥30 g/L in hospitalised decompensated cirrhosis and had more serious adverse events.
- **ANSWER** found improved survival with a specific long-term outpatient albumin regimen in selected patients with cirrhosis/ascites.
- These results are not contradictory prescriptions for every perioperative patient: indication, setting and regimen matter.
- Neither supports routine correction of an isolated low albumin level.
- No routine perioperative dose ceiling does not mean unlimited safe dosing; follow the product, indication and response. [ATTIRE primary trial, 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33657293/) [ANSWER primary trial, 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29861076/)

Advantages of use
Disadvantages (cost, no outcome benefit, overload)
Evidence including SAFE and its quality

A reasoned conclusion on when to use it

items.title: 2010.2 Q5: Fluid management of an infant with intussusception
items.q: A 6-month-old boy presents with an acute abdomen. He is diagnosed with intussusception and booked for laparotomy after a failed attempt at reduction. His heart rate is 160bpm and BP is 75/45 mmHg. His electrolyte profile is as shown: sodium 132 mmol/l (135 – 145), potassium 2.7 mmol/l (3.5 – 5.5), chloride 106 mmol/l (95 – 110), urea 3.3 mmol/l (3.5 – 8.5), creatinine 86 µmol/l (60 – 110), lactate 4.5 mmol/l (1.0 – 1.8). (a) How would you determine his degree of dehydration and how severe is it likely to be? (40%) (b) Describe your perioperative fluid management. (40%) (c) When would you proceed to surgery and why? (20%)
items.model:
> **Examiner report verified:** 2010.2 Q5, pass rate 65.5%. Priorities are age-appropriate interpretation, shock versus dehydration, correct maintenance arithmetic/fluid choice, and reasoned operative timing. Historical practice and contemporary safety requirements are distinguished below.

### (a) Degree of dehydration (40%)

- **History:** duration of vomiting, bilious or not, red-currant jelly stool, oral intake, urine output (nappies), lethargy.
- **Examination:** weight (versus baseline), conscious state and irritability, **capillary refill (over 2 to 3 seconds)**, skin turgor, sunken fontanelle and eyes, dry mucous membranes, peripheries, and the **trend** in heart rate and blood pressure.
- **Investigations:** lactate **4.5 mmol/L** is concerning but nonspecific; sodium 132 and **potassium 2.7 mmol/L** require assessment/monitoring.
  - A creatinine of **86 μmol/L must be interpreted using an infant-specific reference interval** and trend—not the adult-like printed range (60–110) or assumed normal renal function.
  - Obtain glucose, blood gas/base excess, serial electrolytes and urine output.
- **Severity:** HR 160 and BP 75/45 may be compatible with distress and age-related physiology, but **do not exclude compensated shock** in a 6-month-old.
  - Examine CRT, pulse volume, extremity temperature, mentation, weight trend and urine; estimate dehydration from the full picture rather than declaring a precise 5–10% deficit from the stem alone.

### (b) Fluid management (40%)

- **Resuscitation:** IV/IO access and isotonic crystalloid in appropriately sized **10 mL/kg aliquots**, reassessing perfusion; larger or repeated aliquots depend on ongoing losses, heart function, sepsis/obstruction and local paediatric guidance. Blood if haemorrhage is present.
- **Deficit:** estimate from recent weight change and clinical findings; **deficit (mL) = percentage dehydration × weight (kg) × 10** when percentage is written as a whole number.
  - For example, an estimated 5% deficit in a 7-kg infant is 350 mL, not a diagnosis supplied by the stem.
  - Subtract fluid already received and replace according to sodium, perfusion and urgency.
  - Do not enforce a universal “half in eight hours” timetable.
- **Maintenance:** explain the **4–2–1 rule** (for a hypothetical 7–8 kg infant, 28–32 mL/h) but prescribe **balanced isotonic intraoperative maintenance fluid**, adding **1–2% glucose when hypoglycaemia risk warrants it** (this acutely unwell infant needs serial glucose).
  - Postoperatively, use the local isotonic/glucose regimen and reassess rate, losses and stress-related ADH; avoid automatically continuing full maintenance.
  - Healthy older children having short operations do not all require glucose supplementation.
- **Ongoing losses:** **measure** NG/stool/operative losses and replace their water and electrolyte content separately; do not assume a fixed “third-space” mL/kg/h.
- **Potassium:** K 2.7 mmol/L requires ECG, repeated biochemistry, renal function/urine assessment and correction of Mg.
  - With bowel obstruction, IV replacement may be needed: an example RCH ward regimen is **0.2 mmol/kg/h for 3 h (maximum 10 mmol/h)**, with an infusion pump, ECG monitoring for K <3, and repeat K before further replacement.
  - This is an example, not a universal prescription: renal dysfunction and perioperative urgency require paediatric/ICU input and local concentration/access limits.
  - Never give an IV potassium bolus.
- **Intraop:** titrate to measured losses and perfusion; monitor HR/BP/CRT, glucose, gas, Hb, electrolytes and temperature.
- **Postop:** assess ongoing NG losses, renal function and fluid accumulation; use isotonic maintenance/glucose appropriate to risk, consider a reduced basal rate with postoperative ADH, and return to enteral intake when feasible.
  - Monitor urine output (often aiming around 1 mL/kg/h in this infant, interpreted with the full clinical picture), weight and serial biochemistry.

### (c) Timing of surgery (20%)

- Proceed **after immediate resuscitation has improved perfusion and dangerous correctable abnormalities have been addressed as far as time allows**, with a coordinated anaesthetic/surgical plan.
- If perforation, bowel ischaemia or peritonitis is suspected, do not delay time-critical source control: continue resuscitation **during transfer and surgery**, with appropriate monitoring and ICU support.

> **Examiner-focused point:** Allocate time 40% assessment / 40% fluid plan / 20% timing. Distinguish child-specific reference ranges and perfusion findings, name the isotonic fluid/glucose strategy, and avoid unmonitored potassium or unmeasured “third-space” replacement.

items.title: 2007.2 Q6: Circulatory shock: definition and categories of cause
items.q: Define circulatory shock. Categorise the causes of circulatory shock and give an example in each category.
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus:** The original 2007.2 report divides marks evenly between definition and classification with examples. It requires a coherent explanation of inadequate tissue perfusion/oxygen delivery relative to metabolic needs, with consequences for higher marks. Random lists of hypotension causes were inadequate; it specifically criticised general anaesthesia, spinal/epidural anaesthesia and “local shock” from a tourniquet as the examples offered. Use clear pathological examples of circulatory shock.

### Definition (half the answer)

- Circulatory shock is **acute circulatory failure causing inadequate cellular oxygen delivery and/or utilisation relative to metabolic requirements**, resulting in cellular dysfunction and potentially organ failure or death.
- The historical examiner wording emphasised reduced tissue perfusion/oxygen delivery from altered or reduced blood flow.
- Contemporary usage also recognises maldistribution and impaired extraction/utilisation, particularly in sepsis.

- Oxygen delivery depends on cardiac output and arterial oxygen content, predominantly haemoglobin-bound oxygen.
- Falling delivery may initially be offset by increased extraction; when compensation fails, ATP depletion, membrane-pump dysfunction and metabolic disturbance contribute to injury.
- Endothelial leak, microvascular heterogeneity and inflammation can persist after global pressure has improved.
- Metabolic acidosis, altered mentation, oliguria and other organ dysfunction may occur.
- Lactate is a useful adjunct but is neither obligatory nor specific.

**Hypotension alone is not the definition:** compensated shock can exist with a normal BP, while an isolated low BP without impaired perfusion is not automatically shock. A normal saturation does not exclude inadequate delivery from low CO or anaemia.

### Classification with examples (half the answer)

| Category | Main circulatory disturbance | Appropriate pathological examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Hypovolaemic** | Loss of effective circulating volume reduces venous return and stroke volume | Major traumatic haemorrhage; severe gastrointestinal fluid loss with circulatory failure |
| **Cardiogenic** | Pump dysfunction prevents adequate forward flow | Large acute MI with LV failure; acute severe MR from papillary-muscle rupture; myocarditis with low-output shock |
| **Obstructive** | A mechanical barrier impairs cardiac filling or ejection | Cardiac tamponade; tension pneumothorax; high-risk pulmonary embolism |
| **Distributive** | Pathological loss of vascular tone and maldistribution, often with relative hypovolaemia | Septic shock; anaphylactic shock; neurogenic shock after high spinal-cord injury |

- The categories are a framework, not mutually exclusive diagnoses.
- Septic shock may combine vasoplegia, capillary-leak hypovolaemia and myocardial dysfunction; a trauma patient may have bleeding plus tamponade or neurogenic shock.
- Classify by the predominant mechanism while seeking mixed causes.
- Warm/cold peripheries, filling pressures and cardiac output vary with stage and treatment, so they do not provide an infallible category label.

### Stay within the stem

- Give a clear definition, an organised four-category table and at least one defensible example in each.
- This stem does not ask for an extended resuscitation algorithm, every cause of perioperative hypotension or a tourniquet-release essay.
- The physiology explains the definition; concise examples demonstrate the classification. [BJA Education: Vasoactive therapy in shock, 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8212163/) [ESICM circulatory shock and haemodynamic monitoring guideline, 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41236566/)
rubric: Defines acute circulatory failure with tissue/cellular oxygen inadequacy relative to demand
States cellular/organ consequences and distinguishes shock from hypotension alone
Gives hypovolaemic shock with a pathological example
Gives cardiogenic shock with a pathological example
Gives obstructive shock with a pathological example
Gives distributive shock with a pathological example
Recognises mixed mechanisms and avoids the inappropriate examples criticised in the report
Allocates approximately equal effort to definition and classification, without an irrelevant management essay
